chapter: Return to Basie and leaving in 1948
title: Calling Basie from Fort Ord; "Cottage for Sale"; Norman Granz and Lester
summary: From Fort Ord Jones telephoned Basie's band and Milt Ebbins, then visited Lester in Los Angeles, where Norman Granz began helping him.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Basie was in New York City. When I got with

Basie I talked with him at the barbershop in the daytime, which was very difficult to get a phone call through, because we was still at war with Japan. But I finally got Basie. Then Milt Ebbins got on the phone and he says, "Basie's not here. He's in the studio and Billy Eckstine is making a recording." I said, "Well, make 'Cottage for Sale' for me in the key of E flat." So he made it. I said, "Do that for the old soldier boy."

Milt Ebbins was the manager of Basie's band. He was an ex-trumpet player. He had a band like Vaughn Monroe and what have you. He was from the New England states. And it was a gag, going to make a song for poor Jo, GI Jo, and by that time Lester came in - we couldn't get him at Fort Ord but we got him out of the Army some way. Then I went to Los Angeles and I went out to some little hideaway place with Lester and we played. I said, "Don't worry about it, Pres, everything's going to be all right." Norman Granz stepped in and started - he had already started the Jazz at Philharmonic, sure to get Pres some money. You know, he hadn't had no money and he started right there with Norman. Norman loved Lester, you see. Then I said, "Well, pretty soon, Pres, I will be coming out of the Army." When I came out naturally I went back with Basie. Buck didn't go back with Basie.
